page: Amazon Web Services r5ad.2xlarge is a memory-optimized instance running on the AWS Nitro System. It is powered by a first-generation AMD EPYC 7571 processor clocked at 2.2 GHz, offering 8 vCPUs across 4 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading. Memory allocation is generous at 64.0 GB of DDR4 RAM operating at 3 GHz, delivering an 8:1 memory-to-core ratio (8.0 GB per vCPU). The system includes 300 GB of local NVMe SSD instance storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 2 Gbps. It does not include dedicated GPU accelerators.

Benchmark outcomes show that computational speed is constrained compared to modern architectures. The instance scored 727.0 in Geekbench single-core and 2943.0 in multi-core, with stress-ng tests also placing CPU performance in the lower percentiles. Memory bandwidth registered 25.47 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads and 13.03 GB/sec for writes. The PassMark overall CPU score reached 6900.58 and encryption hit 6460.91, both resting in the middle 50% percentile, supported by hardware AES and SHA instructions. However, tasks requiring newer instruction sets, such as AVX-512 or AMX, are not supported by the underlying Zen architecture.

The primary tradeoff of the r5ad.2xlarge is its combination of older compute silicon with high memory density and high-speed local NVMe storage. While raw computational throughput and large-model inference are limited, the hardware profile offers cost-effective access to large DDR4 allocations and low-latency ephemeral disk space. This profile aligns with workloads prioritizing memory footprint and fast scratch space over heavy CPU cycles, including in-memory caches, staging environments, distributed data processing nodes, and intermediate relational database layers.
description: Amazon Web Services r5ad.2xlarge is a memory-optimized virtual machine operating on the Nitro hypervisor. It is configured with an AMD EPYC 7571 processor providing 8 dedicated vCPUs (4 physical cores) at 2.2 GHz, 64.0 GB of DDR4 memory, and a 300 GB local NVMe SSD. Network baseline throughput is 2 Gbps, and no discrete GPUs are included. Performance benchmarks indicate modest single-core and multi-core CPU capacity alongside average encryption throughput, reflecting older Zen architecture limits and the absence of AVX-512 extensions. The server provides strong memory density per core and direct NVMe instance storage, offering a cost-efficient balance for memory-intensive workloads that do not demand cutting-edge processor throughput, such as in-memory caching, memory-bound data processing, and lightweight transactional database engines.
